fetched_contents.text: Comparative effectiveness of warfarin management strategies: a systematic review and network meta-analysis Summary Background The management of warfarin therapy presents clinical challenges due to its narrow therapeutic index. We aimed to evaluate the comparative effectiveness of different management strategies in patients using warfarin. Methods PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL, and EBSCO Open Dissertation were searched from inception to 8 May 2024. Randomized controlled trials that compared the following interventions: patient self-management (PSM), patient self-testing (PST), anticoagulation management services (AMS), and usual care in patients prescribed warfarin for any indication were included. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence interval (CI) were estimated using a random-effects model. Surface under the cumulative ranking curves (SUCRA) were used to rank different interventions. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) online platform. This study is registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023491978). Findings Twenty-eight trials involving 8100 participants were included, with follow-up periods of 1–24 months. Mean warfarin dosages were 4.9–7.2 mg/day. Only PSM showed a significant reduction of major TE risk compared with usual care (RR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.24, 0.71; I2 = 0.0%) with moderate certainty of evidence. The 97.6% SUCRA also supported the beneficial effects of PSM over other interventions. The combined direct and indirect evidence showed significantly higher TTR in PSM compared with usual care (MD = 7.39; 95% CI: 2.39, 12.39), with very low certainty. However, direct evidence showed non-significant TTR improvement (MD = 6.49; 95% CI: −3.09, 16.07, I2 = 96.1%). No differences across various strategies were observed in all-cause mortality, major bleeding, stroke, transient ischemic attack, and hospitalization. Interpretation PSM reduces the risk of major TE events compared with usual care, tends to improve anticoagulation control, and should be considered where appropriate. Funding Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (grant ID 5R18HS027960). Keywords: Anticoagulation management service, Self-management, Self-testing, Self-monitoring, Warfarin ---------------------------------------- Research in context. Evidence before this study Warfarin remains the main anticoagulant used in the treatment and prevention of thrombosis in various medical conditions, especially in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome, mechanical heart valves, and valvular atrial fibrillation (AF), where it has been shown to be more advantageous than direct oral anticoagulants. Several previous studies have highlighted the beneficial effects on anticoagulation control and clinical outcomes of anticoagulation management services (AMS), patient self-testing (PST), and patient self-management (PSM) when compared with usual care. Although a previous network meta-analysis (NMA) has shown the advantageous effects of certain types of self-care on anticoagulation control, it did not consider AMS care separately from usual care. Hence, there is currently a lack of comparative evidence on the effectiveness of different warfarin management strategies. Added value of this study This is the first study to compare the effects of different warfarin management strategies on clinically important outcomes, using both direct and indirect evidence. Our findings have added to the current knowledge regarding the beneficial effects of PSM, demonstrating that it not only reduces the risk of thromboembolic (TE) events when compared with usual care, but also proves to be more effective than AMS. The certainty of evidence generated in our study, together with findings from sensitivity analyses, has supported the robustness of the beneficial effects of PSM program for patients using warfarin. Implications of all the available evidence PSM should be considered for patients who are on warfarin and capable of performing self-management, provided that they receive appropriate support and monitoring from healthcare providers. Further research is needed to gain insight into the adoption of PSM among warfarin users and healthcare providers, and to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of different warfarin management strategies, which could support successful implementation of PSM in practice. Warfarin is the most widely used VKA in many countries globally,1 although there has been a declining trend in its use following the availability of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) since 2010.2 However, warfarin continues to be a vital therapeutic option worldwide.3 In addition to its relatively low cost, warfarin is associated with lower risk of gastrointestinal bleeding4 and all-cause mortality5 compared to some DOACs. fetched_contents.text: Supervised Patient Self-Testing of Warfarin Therapy Using an Online System Abstract Background Point-of-care international normalized ratio (INR) monitoring devices simplify warfarin management by allowing selected patients to monitor their own therapy in their homes. Patient self-testing (PST) has been shown to improve the clinical outcomes of warfarin therapy compared to usual care. Objective To compare management of warfarin therapy using PST combined with online supervision by physicians via a custom system with usual warfarin management, which involved laboratory testing and physician dosing. Methods Interested patients were recruited via community pharmacies to participate in a warfarin PST training program. Participants were required to have a long-term indication for warfarin, have been taking warfarin for at least 6 months, and have Internet access in their home. The training involved two sessions covering theoretical aspects of warfarin therapy, use of the CoaguChek XS, and the study website. Following training, patients monitored their INR once weekly for up to 3 months. Patients and physicians utilized a secure website to communicate INR values, dosage recommendations, and clinical incidents. Physicians provided a 6-12 month history of INR results for comparison with study results. The percentage of time spent within the therapeutic INR range (TTR) was the primary outcome, with participants acting as their own historical controls. The percentage of INR tests in range and participant satisfaction were secondary outcomes. Results Sixteen patients completed training requirements. The mean age of participants was 69.8 (SD 10.1) years. TTR improved significantly from 66.4% to 78.4% during PST (P=.01), and the number of tests within the target range also improved significantly (from 66.0% at prior to the study to 75.9% during PST; P=.04). Patients and physicians expressed a high degree of satisfaction with the monitoring strategy and online system. Conclusions PST supported by an online system for supervision was associated with improved INR control compared to usual care in a small group of elderly patients. Further research is warranted to investigate the clinical outcomes and cost-effectiveness of online systems to support patients monitoring medications and chronic conditions in the home. Keywords: warfarin, self-care, management, international normalized ratio, Internet, communication Introduction Warfarin is an anticoagulant that has been, and continues to be, the standard of care to prevent and treat thromboemboli. It is estimated that between 1% and 2% of the population of the developed world currently receives oral anticoagulants, predominantly warfarin, on a regular basis, mainly for the prevention of ischemic stroke associated with chronic atrial fibrillation. While newer anticoagulants have become available for some indications, their high cost, limited range of indications, and uncertain risk/benefit profile, particularly in the elderly, ensure that debate continues regarding their place in therapy as either replacements or alternatives to warfarin [1-3]. While effective, warfarin is a well-known cause of adverse drug events, and it is fundamental that efforts are made to improve the safety of warfarin therapy and maximize its clinical benefits. Despite decades of clinical use, there are a number of aspects of warfarin therapy that can be targeted to improve patient outcomes. Initial dosing can be optimized through the application of dosing algorithms based on clinical and genetic parameters [4], and patient knowledge of warfarin (often described as suboptimal in the literature) can be improved through health professional intervention [5,6]. Dietary vitamin K intake can be optimized in some patients to improve control [7], and the use of interacting medications can be minimized through judicious prescribing. While the need for regular monitoring of the international normalized ratio (INR), necessitated by large interindividual differences in response to warfarin, can be a burden to patients and health care systems, the ready availability of INR testing means that warfarin therapy can be rigorously monitored to optimize patient safety. The degree of INR control is the major determinant of the efficacy and safety of warfarin therapy [8], and optimized monitoring may make warfarin more clinically effective and cost-effective than its competitors [9,10]. Of course, if warfarin therapy is not well controlled, patients are at increased risk of thrombotic and hemorrhagic complications [11]. Traditionally, warfarin is managed by primary care physicians, pathology providers, or by health professionals in dedicated anticoagulation clinics. Point-of-care (POC) devices offer an accurate alternative to laboratory monitoring [12,13], and their availability has led to an increased focus on patient self-testing (PST) of warfarin. This may comprise self-testing, where the result of the test is communicated to a physician for management (usually by phone), or self-management, where the patient self-adjusts the warfarin dose. PST has been evaluated in a number of well-controlled studies, and a recent meta-analysis demonstrated that self-monitoring of warfarin therapy results in significant reductions in the incidence of thromboembolic complications [14]. The reasons that PST can be more effective than usual care are multifactorial and include enabling an increase in testing frequency, educating patients about important aspects of warfarin therapy, and empowering patients to take a greater role in their own care. It is possible that the appropriate application of information technology could greatly improve warfarin management by improving communication between patients and physicians and facilitating self-monitoring. fetched_contents.text: Self‐monitoring and self‐management of oral anticoagulation Abstract Background The introduction of point‐of‐care devices for the management of patients on oral anticoagulation allows self‐testing by the patient at home. Patients who self‐test can either adjust their medication according to a pre‐determined dose‐INR (international normalized ratio) schedule (self‐management), or they can call a clinic to be told the appropriate dose adjustment (self‐monitoring). Increasing evidence suggests self‐testing of oral anticoagulant therapy is equal to or better than standard monitoring. This is an updated version of the original review published in 2010. Objectives To evaluate the effects on thrombotic events, major haemorrhages, and all‐cause mortality of self‐monitoring or self‐management of oral anticoagulant therapy compared to standard monitoring. Search methods For this review update, we re‐ran the searches of the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), 2015, Issue 6, the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE (Ovid, 1946 to June week 4 2015), Embase (Ovid, 1980 to 2015 week 27) on 1 July 2015. We checked bibliographies and contacted manufacturers and authors of relevant studies. We did not apply any language restrictions . Selection criteria Outcomes analysed were thromboembolic events, mortality, major haemorrhage, minor haemorrhage, tests in therapeutic range, frequency of testing, and feasibility of self‐monitoring and self‐management. Data collection and analysis Review authors independently extracted data and we used a fixed‐effect model with the Mantzel‐Haenzel method to calculate the pooled risk ratio (RR) and Peto’s method to verify the results for uncommon outcomes. We examined heterogeneity amongst studies with the Chi2 and I2 statistics and used GRADE methodology to assess the quality of evidence. Main results We identified 28 randomised trials including 8950 participants (newly incorporated in this update: 10 trials including 4227 participants). The overall quality of the evidence was generally low to moderate. Pooled estimates showed a reduction in thromboembolic events (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.75; participants = 7594; studies = 18; moderate quality of evidence). Both, trials of self‐management or self‐monitoring showed reductions in thromboembolic events (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.70; participants = 3497; studies = 11) and (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.97; participants = 4097; studies = 7), respectively; the quality of evidence for both interventions was moderate. No reduction in all‐cause mortality was found (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.01; participants = 6358; studies = 11; moderate quality of evidence). While self‐management caused a reduction in all‐cause mortality (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.84; participants = 3058; studies = 8); self‐monitoring did not (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.15; participants = 3300; studies = 3); the quality of evidence for both interventions was moderate. In 20 trials (8018 participants) self‐monitoring or self‐management did not reduce major haemorrhage (RR 0.95, 95% CI, 0.80 to 1.12; moderate quality of evidence). There was no significant difference found for minor haemorrhage (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.41; participants = 5365; studies = 13). The quality of evidence was graded as low because of serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 82%). Thromboembolic events were reduced, for both those self‐monitoring or self‐managing oral anticoagulation therapy. A reduction in all‐cause mortality was observed in trials of self‐management but not in self‐monitoring, with no effects on major haemorrhage. Patients who self‐test can either adjust their medication dose according to a pre‐determined dose‐INR schedule (self‐management) or they can call a clinic to be told the appropriate dose adjustment (self‐monitoring). Several published studies and systematic reviews have suggested these methods of monitoring anticoagulation therapy may be equal to or better than standard monitoring by a physician. Study characteristics This is an update of the original review published in 2010. We performed a new search and found 10 new studies (with 4227 participants) to add to the original review, which changed some of the findings. The quality of the evidence was generally low to moderate. Quality of evidence and limitations of the comparisons

Overall evidence strength is mixed and generally limited by study design and the number of trials. The most relevant network meta-analysis included 28 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 8100 participants, which is a substantial sample size, but the evidence is still described as low to moderate for many outcomes and very low for TTR in direct evidence [N1-F1]. A separate review of self-monitoring and self-management of oral anticoagulation also included 28 RCTs with 8950 participants and reported generally low to moderate overall quality of evidence [N4-F3]. This suggests that the literature base is broad enough for meta-analysis, but the certainty of conclusions remains constrained.

The major sources of heterogeneity and inconsistency are several. First, the included trials are not homogeneous in comparator design. The network meta-analysis explicitly notes that direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous (I2 = 96.1%) [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review similarly reports serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 82%) [N4-F3]. Second, the comparators differ substantially by strategy type, with studies comparing patient self-management (PSM), patient self-testing (PST), anticoagulation management services (AMS), and usual care [N1-F1]. Because these strategies differ in how patients are monitored, how adjustments are made, and how much support they receive, direct comparisons across them are not always fair or comparable [N1-F1]. Third, the evidence base includes both direct and indirect comparisons, but the review emphasizes that the direct evidence for TTR was weak, while indirect evidence suggested higher TTR but with very low certainty [N1-F1]. This creates inconsistency between direct and indirect findings and weakens confidence in a single conclusion about the best strategy.

Risk of bias and limitations that weaken conclusions are substantial. The network meta-analysis notes that the certainty of evidence was assessed using CINeMA and that the direct evidence for TTR had very low certainty [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review also reports serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity [N4-F3]. Other limitations include attrition concerns and the fact that self-management requires suitable patients who can be trained and monitored appropriately [N4-R5]. The review also highlights that “attrition may reflect difficulty in managing and sustaining warfarin self-management, and raises the potential of study bias” [N4-R5]. In addition, the comparator arms vary in complexity and intensity, so even when the same outcome is measured, the underlying intervention may differ enough to produce misleading comparisons [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence is strongest for major thromboembolic events and less certain for TTR and bleeding outcomes, with considerable heterogeneity and indirect comparison issues limiting confidence in the ranking of strategies [N1-F1][N4-F3].
node_outputs.N8:
What self-care strategies are most commonly compared and how they differ

The literature most frequently evaluates patient self-management (PSM), patient self-testing (PST), anticoagulation management services (AMS), and usual care as the main comparator arms [N1-F1]. In the network meta-analysis, these four interventions were explicitly included in the search and synthesis, with PSM and PST both being considered forms of self-care [N1-F1]. The review also explicitly notes that a previous network meta-analysis did not separate AMS from usual care, which explains why the current study included AMS as a distinct arm [N1-F1]. In the self-monitoring/self-management review, the interventions were categorized as self-monitoring and self-management, which are closely related but not identical [N4-F3]. The distinction matters because self-management typically involves patients adjusting their own dose according to a pre-determined dose-INR schedule, whereas self-monitoring may involve patients calling a clinic to receive dose advice [N4-F3]. In the supervised PST study, the intervention was described as supervised patient self-testing using an online system, with patients monitoring INR once weekly and communicating results to physicians via a secure website [N2-F2]. That study therefore adds a more structured delivery model compared with simple self-testing.

Each strategy is defined and delivered differently. Usual care typically involves regular in-person clinic visits for INR monitoring and dose adjustments made by healthcare providers [N1-F1]. AMS or anticoagulation clinics offer a more specialized approach with trained healthcare professionals providing INR testing, education, and dose adjustments using a systematic approach [N1-F1]. PST is the patient’s own INR testing, while PSM goes further by allowing the patient to adjust their warfarin dose based on test results [N4-F3][N2-F2]. The supervised PST study combined home INR self-testing with online physician supervision, which is a hybrid model that bridges self-testing with structured support [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a spectrum of self-care strategies: from physician-led usual care, through clinic-based AMS, to self-testing, and finally to self-management with or without remote support [N1-F1][N4-F3][N2-F2].

Comparisons in the literature are direct in some cases and indirect or mixed in others. The network meta-analysis included direct comparisons among the four main strategies [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review also compared self-monitoring and self-management with standard monitoring, which is a direct comparison but still depends on how standard monitoring is defined [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study is a direct comparison of PST with usual warfarin management, which involved laboratory testing and physician dosing [N2-F2]. However, the broader network meta-analysis also used indirect evidence, which explains why direct evidence for TTR was non-significant but indirect evidence suggested higher TTR [N1-F1]. Overall, the strongest direct comparisons are between PSM, PST, AMS, and usual care, while indirect comparisons are plausible when the comparator arms are conceptually related but not directly randomized against one another [N1-F1][N4-F3].
node_outputs.N11:
Comparator-level heterogeneity and indirect comparison issues

Different comparators affect comparability because they differ in intensity, support, and how the INR is managed. Usual care is the most traditional comparator and usually involves in-person monitoring and physician adjustment [N1-F1]. Anticoagulation management services (AMS) add a more structured clinic-based approach with trained professionals [N1-F1]. Patient self-management (PSM) is the most patient-centered comparator because it involves the patient adjusting their own dose based on INR results [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Patient self-testing (PST) is a middle ground where patients test themselves but still rely on a physician for dose advice [N4-F3][N2-F2]. Because these arms differ in how much decision-making is delegated to the patient versus the clinician, they are not equivalent interventions, and outcomes such as TTR may reflect both the strategy itself and the level of support received [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Network meta-analyses and indirect comparisons are plausible in this literature, but their plausibility depends on the similarity of the comparator arms. The network meta-analysis explicitly used both direct and indirect evidence to compare the interventions [N1-F1]. It also noted that previous work had not separated AMS from usual care, so the current study’s inclusion of AMS as a distinct arm was an important methodologic advance [N1-F1]. That said, indirect comparisons are only as credible as the assumptions made about the relationships between comparators. In this case, the network meta-analysis reports that direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous (I2 = 96.1%) [N1-F1]. That high heterogeneity suggests that indirect comparisons may be less reliable than direct comparisons and that the effect estimates are sensitive to how the comparators are grouped [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review also found serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 82%) [N4-F3], further supporting the idea that indirect comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.

Comparator arms that are underrepresented or poorly characterized include more detailed subtypes of self-management and self-testing, as well as strategies that combine technology, patient education, and remote monitoring. The evidence provided here is strongest for PSM, PST, AMS, and usual care, but less explicit about variants such as supervised PST using online systems or hybrid models that combine home testing with periodic clinic review [N2-F2][N4-F3]. The literature also appears to undercharacterize the role of patient education and adherence in comparator definitions, which matters because these are often important determinants of success in self-care strategies [N3 is not provided in the current evidence set, so this conclusion is limited to the supplied material]. Overall, the comparator landscape is sufficiently broad to support network meta-analysis, but the heterogeneity and incomplete characterization of arms mean that indirect comparisons remain imperfect and should not be overinterpreted [N1-F1][N4-F3].
node_outputs.N9:
What the evidence says about effectiveness for TTR and related outcomes

The evidence for TTR suggests that self-care strategies can improve time in therapeutic range, but the magnitude and certainty of the effect vary across studies. The network meta-analysis reported that direct evidence for TTR was non-significant (MD = 6.49; 95% CI: −3.09, 16.07; I2 = 96.1%), while indirect evidence suggested significantly higher TTR compared with usual care (MD = 7.39; 95% CI: 2.39, 12.39), with very low certainty [N1-F1]. In the supervised PST study, TTR improved significantly from 66.4% to 78.4% during PST, representing a mean improvement of 12 percentage points [N2-F2]. The STABLE Results excerpt also reports that weekly testers achieved a TTR of 74% versus 68.9% for variable testers, showing a mean difference of about 5 percentage points [N1-R3]. These findings suggest that self-care strategies, especially more frequent and supervised testing, can increase TTR, but the effect sizes are not consistent across studies and are often modest or uncertain.

Across the compared strategies, PSM and PST appear to be the most frequently associated with improved TTR in the literature. The network meta-analysis explicitly states that PSM tends to improve anticoagulation control [N1-F1], and the self-monitoring/self-management review notes that self-management and self-monitoring both showed reductions in thromboembolic events, with self-management also associated with reductions in all-cause mortality [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study also showed a strong improvement in TTR and tests-in-range, and high participant satisfaction [N2-F2]. However, the literature does not consistently show that one self-care strategy is clearly superior to the others in TTR; instead, the effect depends on the comparator and the setting [N1-F1][N4-F3].

For bleeding and thromboembolism, the evidence is more favorable for thromboembolic risk reduction than for bleeding. The network meta-analysis found that only PSM showed a significant reduction in major thromboembolic events compared with usual care (RR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.24, 0.71; moderate certainty), while direct evidence for TTR was very low certainty [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review similarly found reductions in thromboembolic events for both self-management and self-monitoring, but no reduction in major haemorrhage [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study did not report bleeding events, but the broader literature suggests that self-management can reduce thromboembolism while not necessarily reducing major bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Other studies in the provided evidence also note that home monitoring and management can improve the quality of warfarin therapy without a reduction in major bleeds [N4-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports self-care strategies as potentially safer for thromboembolism than for bleeding, but the safety profile is not uniformly reassuring across all comparisons [N1-F1][N4-F3].
node_outputs.N12:
Practical implications for clinicians and patients

Which strategies are feasible and acceptable in practice? The evidence suggests that self-care strategies can be feasible, but acceptance depends on patient suitability, training, and support. The supervised PST study reported that patients and physicians expressed high satisfaction with the online monitoring strategy, which supports acceptability among at least some patients [N2-F2]. The broader literature also notes that self-management requires suitable patients selected by clinicians, implying that not all patients are equally appropriate candidates [N4-R5]. Guideline recommendations also support a more flexible monitoring schedule for stable patients, which is consistent with the idea that self-care strategies are practical when patients are stable and able to follow a structured regimen [N5-R1][N5-R5]. In other words, supervised self-testing with remote support and structured monitoring appear more feasible than unstructured self-management for many patients, while usual care remains the default for patients who are not yet stable or who require more intensive oversight [N5-R1][N5-R5].

How do guideline recommendations align with the evidence? The guidelines point to a stable INR and reduced monitoring frequency for patients who are well-controlled, which aligns with the evidence that self-care strategies can improve TTR when they are more frequent and structured [N5-R1][N5-R5]. The evidence also supports the idea that self-management and self-testing can improve anticoagulation control, and that these strategies are often compared with usual care [N1-F1][N4-F3]. This means that guideline recommendations are not contradictory to the evidence; rather, they provide a practical framework for when self-care can be considered. However, the evidence also shows that TTR outcomes vary by comparator and that self-care is not universally superior, so guidelines should emphasize selection rather than blanket endorsement [N1-F1][N4-F3].

What caveats should accompany implementation? The main caveats are limited evidence certainty, heterogeneity, and the need for appropriate patient selection. The network meta-analysis and self-monitoring/self-management review both emphasize serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity, which means that the evidence base is strong for major thromboembolic events but weaker for TTR and bleeding outcomes [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous, while indirect evidence suggested a benefit with very low certainty [N1-F1]. This suggests that clinicians should not assume a single strategy is clearly superior and should interpret comparisons cautiously. Another caveat is that self-management requires suitable patients, and study attrition may reflect difficulty in sustaining self-management rather than a flaw in the strategy itself [N4-R5]. Finally, the comparator arms are not homogeneous, so comparisons across studies may not be fully comparable unless the underlying support, training, and monitoring intensity are similar [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Overall, the practical message is that self-care strategies can be effective and acceptable for stable patients, especially when combined with training, supervision, and structured monitoring, but implementation should be guided by patient suitability, guideline-based monitoring thresholds, and awareness of the uncertain evidence base [N5-R1][N5-R5][N1-F1][N4-F3][N4-R5].

Integrated synthesis of how different warfarin self-care strategies compare in effectiveness for TTR and the quality of the evidence

## Summary

The available evidence indicates that different warfarin self-care strategies can improve the time patients spend in the therapeutic INR range (TTR), but the magnitude of improvement, which strategy is most effective, and the certainty of the evidence are not uniform. The strongest overall conclusion is that patient self-management (PSM) and patient self-testing (PST) are the most commonly evaluated self-care strategies, while anticoagulation management services (AMS) and usual care are also frequently used as comparators [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The literature suggests that self-care strategies, especially more frequent and supervised testing, can improve TTR, but the evidence is heterogeneous, limited in certainty for TTR itself, and strongest for major thromboembolic risk reduction rather than bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3][N2-F2]. Overall, the evidence base is large enough to support network meta-analysis, but the quality is mixed and should be interpreted cautiously.

## 1) Which self-care strategies are most commonly compared, and how they differ

The most frequently evaluated strategies are patient self-management (PSM), patient self-testing (PST), anticoagulation management services (AMS), and usual care [N1-F1]. In addition, self-monitoring is often used as a comparator, especially in reviews of oral anticoagulation strategies [N4-F3]. These strategies differ in how much decision-making is delegated to the patient versus the clinician:

- **Usual care** typically involves regular in-person clinic visits for INR monitoring and dose adjustments made by healthcare providers [N1-F1].
- **AMS/anticoagulation clinics** offer a more structured clinic-based approach with trained healthcare professionals providing INR testing, education, and dose adjustments using a systematic approach [N1-F1].
- **PST** is the patient’s own INR testing, while **PSM** goes further by allowing the patient to adjust their warfarin dose based on test results [N4-F3][N2-F2].
- **Self-monitoring** is often described as the patient testing themselves and then calling a clinic for advice, whereas self-management is the patient adjusting their own dose [N4-F3].
- **Supervised PST** adds a hybrid model: home INR self-testing combined with online physician supervision [N2-F2].

Because these arms differ in intensity, support, and monitoring structure, comparisons are not always directly comparable. The network meta-analysis explicitly included direct comparisons among PSM, PST, AMS, and usual care, and also used indirect evidence when direct comparisons were limited [N1-F1]. The supervised PST study is another direct comparison, showing that PST with online support can improve anticoagulation control compared with usual care [N2-F2].

## 2) What the evidence says about effectiveness for TTR and related outcomes

### TTR improvements

The evidence suggests that self-care strategies can improve TTR, but the effect sizes are variable and not always large. The network meta-analysis reported that direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous (I2 = 96.1%), while indirect evidence suggested significantly higher TTR compared with usual care (MD = 7.39; 95% CI: 2.39, 12.39), with very low certainty [N1-F1]. In contrast, the supervised PST study reported a meaningful improvement: TTR increased from 66.4% to 78.4% during PST, representing a mean improvement of 12 percentage points [N2-F2]. The STABLE Results excerpt also found that weekly testers achieved a TTR of 74% versus 68.9% for variable testers, a mean difference of about 5 percentage points [N1-R3].

### Which strategies appear most effective for maintaining TTR in range

Across the evidence base, **PSM and PST** appear most frequently associated with improved TTR. The network meta-analysis found that PSM tends to improve anticoagulation control [N1-F1], and the self-monitoring/self-management review found that self-management and self-monitoring both showed reductions in thromboembolic events, with self-management also associated with reductions in all-cause mortality [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study also showed a strong improvement in TTR and tests-in-range, as well as high participant satisfaction [N2-F2]. However, the literature does not consistently show that one self-care strategy is clearly superior to the others in TTR; instead, the effect depends on the comparator and setting [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### Effects on bleeding, thromboembolism, and other harms

The evidence is more favorable for thromboembolic risk reduction than for bleeding. The network meta-analysis found that only PSM showed a significant reduction in major thromboembolic events compared with usual care (RR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.24, 0.71; moderate certainty), while direct evidence for TTR was very low certainty [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review similarly found reductions in thromboembolic events for both self-management and self-monitoring, but no reduction in major haemorrhage [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study did not report bleeding events, but the broader literature suggests that self-management can reduce thromboembolism while not necessarily reducing major bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Other evidence also notes that home monitoring and management can improve the quality of warfarin therapy without a reduction in major bleeds [N4-F3].

## 3) Quality of the evidence

The quality of evidence is mixed and generally limited. The most relevant network meta-analysis included 28 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 8100 participants, which is a large sample, but the evidence is still described as low to moderate for many outcomes and very low for TTR in direct evidence [N1-F1]. A separate review of self-monitoring and self-management of oral anticoagulation also included 28 RCTs with 8950 participants and reported generally low to moderate overall quality of evidence [N4-F3]. This means the literature is broad enough for meta-analysis, but the certainty of conclusions remains constrained.

Major sources of heterogeneity and inconsistency include:

- **Comparator heterogeneity**: The studies compare different strategies with different levels of support, monitoring, and patient involvement, so direct comparisons are not always fair or comparable [N1-F1].
- **Heterogeneity in outcomes**: The direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous (I2 = 96.1%) [N1-F1].
- **Risk of bias and study limitations**: The evidence base includes serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity, which weakens conclusions [N4-F3]. Attrition concerns also raise the potential for study bias, particularly in self-management studies [N4-R5].

## 4) Comparator-level heterogeneity and indirect comparison issues

Different comparators affect comparability because they differ in intensity, support, and how the INR is managed. Usual care is the most traditional comparator and usually involves in-person monitoring and physician adjustment [N1-F1]. AMS adds a more structured clinic-based approach with trained professionals [N1-F1]. PSM is the most patient-centered comparator because it involves the patient adjusting their own dose based on INR results [N1-F1][N4-F3]. PST is a middle ground where patients test themselves but still rely on a physician for dose advice [N4-F3][N2-F2]. Because these arms differ in how much decision-making is delegated, they are not equivalent interventions, and outcomes such as TTR may reflect both the strategy itself and the level of support received [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Network meta-analyses and indirect comparisons are plausible in this literature, but only if the comparator arms are sufficiently similar. The network meta-analysis explicitly used both direct and indirect evidence to compare the interventions [N1-F1]. However, indirect comparisons are only as credible as the assumptions made about the relationships between comparators. In this case, the direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous, which suggests that indirect comparisons should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review also found serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 82%) [N4-F3], further supporting caution in interpreting indirect comparisons.

Comparator arms that are underrepresented or poorly characterized include more detailed subtypes of self-management and self-testing, as well as strategies that combine technology, patient education, and remote monitoring. The evidence provided here is strongest for PSM, PST, AMS, and usual care, but less explicit about variants such as supervised PST using online systems or hybrid models that combine home testing with periodic clinic review [N2-F2][N4-F3]. The comparator landscape is sufficiently broad to support network meta-analysis, but the heterogeneity and incomplete characterization of arms mean that indirect comparisons remain imperfect and should not be overinterpreted [N1-F1][N4-F3].

## 5) Practical implications for clinicians and patients

### Which strategies are feasible and acceptable in practice?

The evidence suggests that self-care strategies can be feasible, but acceptance depends on patient suitability, training, and support. The supervised PST study reported that patients and physicians expressed high satisfaction with the online monitoring strategy, which supports acceptability among at least some patients [N2-F2]. The broader literature also notes that self-management requires suitable patients selected by clinicians, implying that not all patients are equally appropriate candidates [N4-R5]. Guideline recommendations also support a more flexible monitoring schedule for stable patients, which is consistent with the idea that self-care strategies are practical when patients are stable and able to follow a structured regimen [N5-R1][N5-R5].

### How do guideline recommendations align with the evidence?

Guidelines point to a stable INR and reduced monitoring frequency for patients who are well-controlled, which aligns with the evidence that self-care strategies can improve TTR when they are more frequent and structured [N5-R1][N5-R5]. The evidence also supports the idea that self-management and self-testing can improve anticoagulation control, and that these strategies are often compared with usual care [N1-F1][N4-F3]. This means that guideline recommendations are not contradictory to the evidence; rather, they provide a practical framework for when self-care can be considered. However, the evidence also shows that TTR outcomes vary by comparator and that self-care is not universally superior, so guidelines should emphasize selection rather than blanket endorsement [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### What caveats should accompany implementation?

The main caveats are limited evidence certainty, heterogeneity, and the need for appropriate patient selection. The network meta-analysis and self-monitoring/self-management review both emphasize serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity, which means the evidence base is strong for major thromboembolic events but weaker for TTR and bleeding outcomes [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous, while indirect evidence suggested a benefit with very low certainty [N1-F1]. This suggests clinicians should not assume a single strategy is clearly superior and should interpret comparisons cautiously. Another caveat is that self-management requires suitable patients, and study attrition may reflect difficulty in sustaining self-management rather than a flaw in the strategy itself [N4-R5]. Finally, the comparator arms are not homogeneous, so comparisons across studies may not be fully comparable unless the underlying support, training, and monitoring intensity are similar [N1-F1][N4-F3].

## 6) Bottom line

Overall, the evidence supports the idea that **warfarin self-care strategies can improve TTR**, especially when they are more frequent, supervised, or combined with remote support [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, **the quality of evidence is mixed and limited**, with substantial heterogeneity and serious risk of bias, particularly for TTR itself [N1-F1][N4-F3]. **PSM and PST appear most frequently associated with improved TTR**, but they are not clearly superior to each other in all studies [N1-F1][N4-F3]. **Thromboembolic risk reduction is more consistently supported than bleeding reduction**, and the evidence is stronger for major thromboembolic events than for major bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Clinicians and patients should therefore treat self-care strategies as a **practical option for stable patients**, but not as a one-size-fits-all solution, and should be cautious about overinterpreting indirect comparisons or assuming superior effectiveness across all settings [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-R1][N5-R5].

## Summary

The available evidence indicates that different warfarin self-care strategies can improve the time patients spend in the therapeutic INR range (TTR), but the magnitude of improvement, which strategy is most effective, and the certainty of the evidence are not uniform. The strongest overall conclusion is that patient self-management (PSM) and patient self-testing (PST) are the most commonly evaluated self-care strategies, while anticoagulation management services (AMS) and usual care are also frequently used as comparators [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The literature suggests that self-care strategies, especially more frequent and supervised testing, can improve TTR, but the evidence is heterogeneous, limited in certainty for TTR itself, and strongest for major thromboembolic risk reduction rather than bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3][N2-F2]. Overall, the evidence base is large enough to support network meta-analysis, but the quality is mixed and should be interpreted cautiously.

## 1) Which self-care strategies are most commonly compared, and how they differ

The most frequently evaluated strategies are patient self-management (PSM), patient self-testing (PST), anticoagulation management services (AMS), and usual care [N1-F1]. In addition, self-monitoring is often used as a comparator, especially in reviews of oral anticoagulation strategies [N4-F3]. These strategies differ in how much decision-making is delegated to the patient versus the clinician:

- **Usual care** typically involves regular in-person clinic visits for INR monitoring and dose adjustments made by healthcare providers [N1-F1].
- **AMS/anticoagulation clinics** offer a more structured clinic-based approach with trained healthcare professionals providing INR testing, education, and dose adjustments using a systematic approach [N1-F1].
- **PST** is the patient’s own INR testing, while **PSM** goes further by allowing the patient to adjust their warfarin dose based on test results [N4-F3][N2-F2].
- **Self-monitoring** is often described as the patient testing themselves and then calling a clinic for advice, whereas self-management is the patient adjusting their own dose [N4-F3].
- **Supervised PST** adds a hybrid model: home INR self-testing combined with online physician supervision [N2-F2].

Because these arms differ in intensity, support, and monitoring structure, comparisons are not always directly comparable. The network meta-analysis explicitly included direct comparisons among PSM, PST, AMS, and usual care, and also used indirect evidence when direct comparisons were limited [N1-F1]. The supervised PST study is another direct comparison, showing that PST with online support can improve anticoagulation control compared with usual care [N2-F2].

## 2) What the evidence says about effectiveness for TTR and related outcomes

### TTR improvements

The evidence suggests that self-care strategies can improve TTR, but the effect sizes are variable and not always large. The network meta-analysis reported that direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous (I2 = 96.1%), while indirect evidence suggested significantly higher TTR compared with usual care (MD = 7.39; 95% CI: 2.39, 12.39), with very low certainty [N1-F1]. In contrast, the supervised PST study reported a meaningful improvement: TTR increased from 66.4% to 78.4% during PST, representing a mean improvement of 12 percentage points [N2-F2]. The STABLE Results excerpt also found that weekly testers achieved a TTR of 74% versus 68.9% for variable testers, a mean difference of about 5 percentage points [N1-R3].

### Which strategies appear most effective for maintaining TTR in range

Across the evidence base, **PSM and PST** appear most frequently associated with improved TTR. The network meta-analysis found that PSM tends to improve anticoagulation control [N1-F1], and the self-monitoring/self-management review found that self-management and self-monitoring both showed reductions in thromboembolic events, with self-management also associated with reductions in all-cause mortality [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study also showed a strong improvement in TTR and tests-in-range, as well as high participant satisfaction [N2-F2]. However, the literature does not consistently show that one self-care strategy is clearly superior to the others in TTR; instead, the effect depends on the comparator and setting [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### Effects on bleeding, thromboembolism, and other harms

The evidence is more favorable for thromboembolic risk reduction than for bleeding. The network meta-analysis found that only PSM showed a significant reduction in major thromboembolic events compared with usual care (RR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.24, 0.71; moderate certainty), while direct evidence for TTR was very low certainty [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review similarly found reductions in thromboembolic events for both self-management and self-monitoring, but no reduction in major haemorrhage [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study did not report bleeding events, but the broader literature suggests that self-management can reduce thromboembolism while not necessarily reducing major bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Other evidence also notes that home monitoring and management can improve the quality of warfarin therapy without a reduction in major bleeds [N4-F3].

## 3) Quality of the evidence

The quality of evidence is mixed and generally limited. The most relevant network meta-analysis included 28 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 8100 participants, which is a large sample, but the evidence is still described as low to moderate for many outcomes and very low for TTR in direct evidence [N1-F1]. A separate review of self-monitoring and self-management of oral anticoagulation also included 28 RCTs with 8950 participants and reported generally low to moderate overall quality of evidence [N4-F3]. This means the literature is broad enough for meta-analysis, but the certainty of conclusions remains constrained.

Major sources of heterogeneity and inconsistency include:

- **Comparator heterogeneity**: The studies compare different strategies with different levels of support, monitoring, and patient involvement, so direct comparisons are not always fair or comparable [N1-F1].
- **Heterogeneity in outcomes**: The direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous (I2 = 96.1%) [N1-F1].
- **Risk of bias and study limitations**: The evidence base includes serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity, which weakens conclusions [N4-F3]. Attrition concerns also raise the potential for study bias, particularly in self-management studies [N4-R5].

## 4) Comparator-level heterogeneity and indirect comparison issues

Different comparators affect comparability because they differ in intensity, support, and how the INR is managed. Usual care is the most traditional comparator and usually involves in-person monitoring and physician adjustment [N1-F1]. AMS adds a more structured clinic-based approach with trained professionals [N1-F1]. Network meta-analyses and indirect comparisons are plausible in this literature, but only if the comparator arms are sufficiently similar. The network meta-analysis explicitly used both direct and indirect evidence to compare the interventions [N1-F1]. However, indirect comparisons are only as credible as the assumptions made about the relationships between comparators. In this case, the direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous, which suggests that indirect comparisons should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review also found serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 82%) [N4-F3], further supporting caution in interpreting indirect comparisons.

Comparator arms that are underrepresented or poorly characterized include more detailed subtypes of self-management and self-testing, as well as strategies that combine technology, patient education, and remote monitoring. ## 5) Practical implications for clinicians and patients

### Which strategies are feasible and acceptable in practice?

The evidence suggests that self-care strategies can be feasible, but acceptance depends on patient suitability, training, and support. The supervised PST study reported that patients and physicians expressed high satisfaction with the online monitoring strategy, which supports acceptability among at least some patients [N2-F2]. The evidence also supports the idea that self-management and self-testing can improve anticoagulation control, and that these strategies are often compared with usual care [N1-F1][N4-F3]. This means that guideline recommendations are not contradictory to the evidence; rather, they provide a practical framework for when self-care can be considered. However, the evidence also shows that TTR outcomes vary by comparator and that self-care is not universally superior, so guidelines should emphasize selection rather than blanket endorsement [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### What caveats should accompany implementation?

The main caveats are limited evidence certainty, heterogeneity, and the need for appropriate patient selection. The network meta-analysis and self-monitoring/self-management review both emphasize serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity, which means the evidence base is strong for major thromboembolic events but weaker for TTR and bleeding outcomes [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous, while indirect evidence suggested a benefit with very low certainty [N1-F1]. This suggests clinicians should not assume a single strategy is clearly superior and should interpret comparisons cautiously. Another caveat is that self-management requires suitable patients, and study attrition may reflect difficulty in sustaining self-management rather than a flaw in the strategy itself [N4-R5]. Finally, the comparator arms are not homogeneous, so comparisons across studies may not be fully comparable unless the underlying support, training, and monitoring intensity are similar [N1-F1][N4-F3].

## 6) Bottom line

Overall, the evidence supports the idea that **warfarin self-care strategies can improve TTR**, especially when they are more frequent, supervised, or combined with remote support [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, **the quality of evidence is mixed and limited**, with substantial heterogeneity and serious risk of bias, particularly for TTR itself [N1-F1][N4-F3]. **PSM and PST appear most frequently associated with improved TTR**, but they are not clearly superior to each other in all studies [N1-F1][N4-F3]. **Thromboembolic risk reduction is more consistently supported than bleeding reduction**, and the evidence is stronger for major thromboembolic events than for major bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Clinicians and patients should therefore treat self-care strategies as a **practical option for stable patients**, but not as a one-size-fits-all solution, and should be cautious about overinterpreting indirect comparisons or assuming superior effectiveness across all settings [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-R1][N5-R5].

Quality of evidence and limitations of the comparisons

Overall evidence strength is mixed and generally limited by study design and the number of trials. The most relevant network meta-analysis included 28 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 8100 participants, which is a substantial sample size, but the evidence is still described as low to moderate for many outcomes and very low for TTR in direct evidence [N1-F1]. A separate review of self-monitoring and self-management of oral anticoagulation also included 28 RCTs with 8950 participants and reported generally low to moderate overall quality of evidence [N4-F3]. This suggests that the literature base is broad enough for meta-analysis, but the certainty of conclusions remains constrained.

The major sources of heterogeneity and inconsistency are several. First, the included trials are not homogeneous in comparator design. The network meta-analysis explicitly notes that direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous (I2 = 96.1%) [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review similarly reports serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 82%) [N4-F3]. Second, the comparators differ substantially by strategy type, with studies comparing patient self-management (PSM), patient self-testing (PST), anticoagulation management services (AMS), and usual care [N1-F1]. Because these strategies differ in how patients are monitored, how adjustments are made, and how much support they receive, direct comparisons across them are not always fair or comparable [N1-F1]. Third, the evidence base includes both direct and indirect comparisons, but the review emphasizes that the direct evidence for TTR was weak, while indirect evidence suggested higher TTR but with very low certainty [N1-F1]. This creates inconsistency between direct and indirect findings and weakens confidence in a single conclusion about the best strategy.

Risk of bias and limitations that weaken conclusions are substantial. The network meta-analysis notes that the certainty of evidence was assessed using CINeMA and that the direct evidence for TTR had very low certainty [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review also reports serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity [N4-F3]. Other limitations include attrition concerns and the fact that self-management requires suitable patients who can be trained and monitored appropriately [N4-R5]. The review also highlights that “attrition may reflect difficulty in managing and sustaining warfarin self-management, and raises the potential of study bias” [N4-R5]. In addition, the comparator arms vary in complexity and intensity, so even when the same outcome is measured, the underlying intervention may differ enough to produce misleading comparisons [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence is strongest for major thromboembolic events and less certain for TTR and bleeding outcomes, with considerable heterogeneity and indirect comparison issues limiting confidence in the ranking of strategies [N1-F1][N4-F3].

In the network meta-analysis, these four interventions were explicitly included in the search and synthesis, with PSM and PST both being considered forms of self-care [N1-F1]. The review also explicitly notes that a previous network meta-analysis did not separate AMS from usual care, which explains why the current study included AMS as a distinct arm [N1-F1]. In the self-monitoring/self-management review, the interventions were categorized as self-monitoring and self-management, which are closely related but not identical [N4-F3]. The distinction matters because self-management typically involves patients adjusting their own dose according to a pre-determined dose-INR schedule, whereas self-monitoring may involve patients calling a clinic to receive dose advice [N4-F3]. In the supervised PST study, the intervention was described as supervised patient self-testing using an online system, with patients monitoring INR once weekly and communicating results to physicians via a secure website [N2-F2]. That study therefore adds a more structured delivery model compared with simple self-testing.

Each strategy is defined and delivered differently. Usual care typically involves regular in-person clinic visits for INR monitoring and dose adjustments made by healthcare providers [N1-F1]. AMS or anticoagulation clinics offer a more specialized approach with trained healthcare professionals providing INR testing, education, and dose adjustments using a systematic approach [N1-F1]. PST is the patient’s own INR testing, while PSM goes further by allowing the patient to adjust their warfarin dose based on test results [N4-F3][N2-F2]. The supervised PST study combined home INR self-testing with online physician supervision, which is a hybrid model that bridges self-testing with structured support [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a spectrum of self-care strategies: from physician-led usual care, through clinic-based AMS, to self-testing, and finally to self-management with or without remote support [N1-F1][N4-F3][N2-F2].

Comparisons in the literature are direct in some cases and indirect or mixed in others. The network meta-analysis included direct comparisons among the four main strategies [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review also compared self-monitoring and self-management with standard monitoring, which is a direct comparison but still depends on how standard monitoring is defined [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study is a direct comparison of PST with usual warfarin management, which involved laboratory testing and physician dosing [N2-F2]. However, the broader network meta-analysis also used indirect evidence, which explains why direct evidence for TTR was non-significant but indirect evidence suggested higher TTR [N1-F1]. Overall, the strongest direct comparisons are between PSM, PST, AMS, and usual care, while indirect comparisons are plausible when the comparator arms are conceptually related but not directly randomized against one another [N1-F1][N4-F3].

What the evidence says about effectiveness for TTR and related outcomes

The evidence for TTR suggests that self-care strategies can improve time in therapeutic range, but the magnitude and certainty of the effect vary across studies. The network meta-analysis reported that direct evidence for TTR was non-significant (MD = 6.49; 95% CI: −3.09, 16.07; I2 = 96.1%), while indirect evidence suggested significantly higher TTR compared with usual care (MD = 7.39; 95% CI: 2.39, 12.39), with very low certainty [N1-F1]. In the supervised PST study, TTR improved significantly from 66.4% to 78.4% during PST, representing a mean improvement of 12 percentage points [N2-F2]. The STABLE Results excerpt also reports that weekly testers achieved a TTR of 74% versus 68.9% for variable testers, showing a mean difference of about 5 percentage points [N1-R3]. These findings suggest that self-care strategies, especially more frequent and supervised testing, can increase TTR, but the effect sizes are not consistent across studies and are often modest or uncertain.

Across the compared strategies, PSM and PST appear to be the most frequently associated with improved TTR in the literature. The network meta-analysis explicitly states that PSM tends to improve anticoagulation control [N1-F1], and the self-monitoring/self-management review notes that self-management and self-monitoring both showed reductions in thromboembolic events, with self-management also associated with reductions in all-cause mortality [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study also showed a strong improvement in TTR and tests-in-range, and high participant satisfaction [N2-F2]. However, the literature does not consistently show that one self-care strategy is clearly superior to the others in TTR; instead, the effect depends on the comparator and the setting [N1-F1][N4-F3].

For bleeding and thromboembolism, the evidence is more favorable for thromboembolic risk reduction than for bleeding. The network meta-analysis found that only PSM showed a significant reduction in major thromboembolic events compared with usual care (RR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.24, 0.71; moderate certainty), while direct evidence for TTR was very low certainty [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review similarly found reductions in thromboembolic events for both self-management and self-monitoring, but no reduction in major haemorrhage [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study did not report bleeding events, but the broader literature suggests that self-management can reduce thromboembolism while not necessarily reducing major bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Other studies in the provided evidence also note that home monitoring and management can improve the quality of warfarin therapy without a reduction in major bleeds [N4-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports self-care strategies as potentially safer for thromboembolism than for bleeding, but the safety profile is not uniformly reassuring across all comparisons [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Integrated synthesis of how different warfarin self-care strategies compare in effectiveness for TTR and the quality of the evidence

## Summary

The available evidence indicates that different warfarin self-care strategies can improve the time patients spend in the therapeutic INR range (TTR), but the magnitude of improvement, which strategy is most effective, and the certainty of the evidence are not uniform. The strongest overall conclusion is that patient self-management (PSM) and patient self-testing (PST) are the most commonly evaluated self-care strategies, while anticoagulation management services (AMS) and usual care are also frequently used as comparators [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The literature suggests that self-care strategies, especially more frequent and supervised testing, can improve TTR, but the evidence is heterogeneous, limited in certainty for TTR itself, and strongest for major thromboembolic risk reduction rather than bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3][N2-F2]. Overall, the evidence base is large enough to support network meta-analysis, but the quality is mixed and should be interpreted cautiously.

## 1) Which self-care strategies are most commonly compared, and how they differ

The most frequently evaluated strategies are patient self-management (PSM), patient self-testing (PST), anticoagulation management services (AMS), and usual care [N1-F1]. In addition, self-monitoring is often used as a comparator, especially in reviews of oral anticoagulation strategies [N4-F3]. These strategies differ in how much decision-making is delegated to the patient versus the clinician:

- **Usual care** typically involves regular in-person clinic visits for INR monitoring and dose adjustments made by healthcare providers [N1-F1].
- **AMS/anticoagulation clinics** offer a more structured clinic-based approach with trained healthcare professionals providing INR testing, education, and dose adjustments using a systematic approach [N1-F1].
- **PST** is the patient’s own INR testing, while **PSM** goes further by allowing the patient to adjust their warfarin dose based on test results [N4-F3][N2-F2].
- **Self-monitoring** is often described as the patient testing themselves and then calling a clinic for advice, whereas self-management is the patient adjusting their own dose [N4-F3].
- **Supervised PST** adds a hybrid model: home INR self-testing combined with online physician supervision [N2-F2].

Because these arms differ in intensity, support, and monitoring structure, comparisons are not always directly comparable. The network meta-analysis explicitly included direct comparisons among PSM, PST, AMS, and usual care, and also used indirect evidence when direct comparisons were limited [N1-F1]. The supervised PST study is another direct comparison, showing that PST with online support can improve anticoagulation control compared with usual care [N2-F2].

## 2) What the evidence says about effectiveness for TTR and related outcomes

### TTR improvements

The evidence suggests that self-care strategies can improve TTR, but the effect sizes are variable and not always large. The network meta-analysis reported that direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous (I2 = 96.1%), while indirect evidence suggested significantly higher TTR compared with usual care (MD = 7.39; 95% CI: 2.39, 12.39), with very low certainty [N1-F1]. In contrast, the supervised PST study reported a meaningful improvement: TTR increased from 66.4% to 78.4% during PST, representing a mean improvement of 12 percentage points [N2-F2]. The STABLE Results excerpt also found that weekly testers achieved a TTR of 74% versus 68.9% for variable testers, a mean difference of about 5 percentage points [N1-R3].

### Which strategies appear most effective for maintaining TTR in range

Across the evidence base, **PSM and PST** appear most frequently associated with improved TTR. The network meta-analysis found that PSM tends to improve anticoagulation control [N1-F1], and the self-monitoring/self-management review found that self-management and self-monitoring both showed reductions in thromboembolic events, with self-management also associated with reductions in all-cause mortality [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study also showed a strong improvement in TTR and tests-in-range, as well as high participant satisfaction [N2-F2]. However, the literature does not consistently show that one self-care strategy is clearly superior to the others in TTR; instead, the effect depends on the comparator and setting [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### Effects on bleeding, thromboembolism, and other harms

The evidence is more favorable for thromboembolic risk reduction than for bleeding. The network meta-analysis found that only PSM showed a significant reduction in major thromboembolic events compared with usual care (RR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.24, 0.71; moderate certainty), while direct evidence for TTR was very low certainty [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review similarly found reductions in thromboembolic events for both self-management and self-monitoring, but no reduction in major haemorrhage [N4-F3]. The supervised PST study did not report bleeding events, but the broader literature suggests that self-management can reduce thromboembolism while not necessarily reducing major bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Other evidence also notes that home monitoring and management can improve the quality of warfarin therapy without a reduction in major bleeds [N4-F3].

## 3) Quality of the evidence

The quality of evidence is mixed and generally limited. The most relevant network meta-analysis included 28 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 8100 participants, which is a large sample, but the evidence is still described as low to moderate for many outcomes and very low for TTR in direct evidence [N1-F1]. A separate review of self-monitoring and self-management of oral anticoagulation also included 28 RCTs with 8950 participants and reported generally low to moderate overall quality of evidence [N4-F3]. This means the literature is broad enough for meta-analysis, but the certainty of conclusions remains constrained.

Major sources of heterogeneity and inconsistency include:

- **Comparator heterogeneity**: The studies compare different strategies with different levels of support, monitoring, and patient involvement, so direct comparisons are not always fair or comparable [N1-F1].
- **Heterogeneity in outcomes**: The direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous (I2 = 96.1%) [N1-F1].
- **Risk of bias and study limitations**: The evidence base includes serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity, which weakens conclusions [N4-F3]. Attrition concerns also raise the potential for study bias, particularly in self-management studies [N4-R5].

## 4) Comparator-level heterogeneity and indirect comparison issues

Different comparators affect comparability because they differ in intensity, support, and how the INR is managed. Usual care is the most traditional comparator and usually involves in-person monitoring and physician adjustment [N1-F1]. AMS adds a more structured clinic-based approach with trained professionals [N1-F1]. PSM is the most patient-centered comparator because it involves the patient adjusting their own dose based on INR results [N1-F1][N4-F3]. PST is a middle ground where patients test themselves but still rely on a physician for dose advice [N4-F3][N2-F2]. Because these arms differ in how much decision-making is delegated, they are not equivalent interventions, and outcomes such as TTR may reflect both the strategy itself and the level of support received [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Network meta-analyses and indirect comparisons are plausible in this literature, but only if the comparator arms are sufficiently similar. The network meta-analysis explicitly used both direct and indirect evidence to compare the interventions [N1-F1]. However, indirect comparisons are only as credible as the assumptions made about the relationships between comparators. In this case, the direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous, which suggests that indirect comparisons should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1]. The self-monitoring/self-management review also found serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 82%) [N4-F3], further supporting caution in interpreting indirect comparisons.

Comparator arms that are underrepresented or poorly characterized include more detailed subtypes of self-management and self-testing, as well as strategies that combine technology, patient education, and remote monitoring. The evidence provided here is strongest for PSM, PST, AMS, and usual care, but less explicit about variants such as supervised PST using online systems or hybrid models that combine home testing with periodic clinic review [N2-F2][N4-F3]. The comparator landscape is sufficiently broad to support network meta-analysis, but the heterogeneity and incomplete characterization of arms mean that indirect comparisons remain imperfect and should not be overinterpreted [N1-F1][N4-F3].

## 5) Practical implications for clinicians and patients

### Which strategies are feasible and acceptable in practice?

The evidence suggests that self-care strategies can be feasible, but acceptance depends on patient suitability, training, and support. The supervised PST study reported that patients and physicians expressed high satisfaction with the online monitoring strategy, which supports acceptability among at least some patients [N2-F2]. The broader literature also notes that self-management requires suitable patients selected by clinicians, implying that not all patients are equally appropriate candidates [N4-R5]. Guideline recommendations also support a more flexible monitoring schedule for stable patients, which is consistent with the idea that self-care strategies are practical when patients are stable and able to follow a structured regimen [N5-R1][N5-R5].

### How do guideline recommendations align with the evidence?

Guidelines point to a stable INR and reduced monitoring frequency for patients who are well-controlled, which aligns with the evidence that self-care strategies can improve TTR when they are more frequent and structured [N5-R1][N5-R5]. The evidence also supports the idea that self-management and self-testing can improve anticoagulation control, and that these strategies are often compared with usual care [N1-F1][N4-F3]. This means that guideline recommendations are not contradictory to the evidence; rather, they provide a practical framework for when self-care can be considered. However, the evidence also shows that TTR outcomes vary by comparator and that self-care is not universally superior, so guidelines should emphasize selection rather than blanket endorsement [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### What caveats should accompany implementation?

The main caveats are limited evidence certainty, heterogeneity, and the need for appropriate patient selection. The network meta-analysis and self-monitoring/self-management review both emphasize serious risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity, which means the evidence base is strong for major thromboembolic events but weaker for TTR and bleeding outcomes [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The direct evidence for TTR was non-significant and highly heterogeneous, while indirect evidence suggested a benefit with very low certainty [N1-F1]. This suggests clinicians should not assume a single strategy is clearly superior and should interpret comparisons cautiously. Another caveat is that self-management requires suitable patients, and study attrition may reflect difficulty in sustaining self-management rather than a flaw in the strategy itself [N4-R5]. Finally, the comparator arms are not homogeneous, so comparisons across studies may not be fully comparable unless the underlying support, training, and monitoring intensity are similar [N1-F1][N4-F3].

## 6) Bottom line

Overall, the evidence supports the idea that **warfarin self-care strategies can improve TTR**, especially when they are more frequent, supervised, or combined with remote support [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, **the quality of evidence is mixed and limited**, with substantial heterogeneity and serious risk of bias, particularly for TTR itself [N1-F1][N4-F3]. **PSM and PST appear most frequently associated with improved TTR**, but they are not clearly superior to each other in all studies [N1-F1][N4-F3]. **Thromboembolic risk reduction is more consistently supported than bleeding reduction**, and the evidence is stronger for major thromboembolic events than for major bleeding [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Clinicians and patients should therefore treat self-care strategies as a **practical option for stable patients**, but not as a one-size-fits-all solution, and should be cautious about overinterpreting indirect comparisons or assuming superior effectiveness across all settings [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-R1][N5-R5].
